items.q: What problem does DDD actually solve? What does ubiquitous language really mean?
items.a:
DDD [[r:is not]] a catalog of patterns to copy. It solves a [[o:communication]] problem: the business uses one vocabulary, the code uses another, and every translation between them is another opportunity for bugs. **Ubiquitous language** = *one* shared vocabulary used by developers, BAs, QA, and domain experts — and [[g:represented verbatim in the code]]. 
// The business says: "hold a seat", "issue a ticket", "refund a ticket"
//
// WRONG — technical vocabulary that must be translated at every meeting
bookingService.updateStatus(id, 2);
bookingRepository.setFlag(id, true);
//
// RIGHT — reads exactly like a sentence the business uses
booking.holdSeat(seatNo);
booking.issueTicket(gdsRef);
booking.refund(reason);
A simple test: [[o:read a method aloud to a domain expert]]. If they understand it immediately → the language is shared. If you have to explain that "status 2 means the seat is held" → it is not shared yet. **But the language is consistent only within a [[b:bounded context]]** — not across the entire company. That is the subject of 24.2. :::warn The biggest trap DDD [[r:is not]] "having a `domain` directory" or "using `@Entity`". Many projects claim to practice DDD but are really layered architecture with renamed directories: entities have only getters and setters, while every rule lives in a `Service` (12.11 anemic domain). Directory structure is not DDD; modeling is. ::: :::deep - DDD has a cost: it requires [[g:a domain expert working closely with the team]]. Without one, everything else is ceremony — this is a prerequisite that books are often skimmed past. - Separate its two parts clearly: [[o:strategic design]] (dividing contexts and drawing maps — the highest-value part, which everyone should know) and [[o:tactical design]] (aggregates, VOs, and repositories — worth the cost only in the core domain). - Classify subdomains to decide where to invest: [[g:core]] (competitive advantage — engineer it carefully and apply DDD here), [[g:supporting]] (necessary but not differentiating — keep it simple), and [[g:generic]] (sending email, generating PDFs — buy it or use a library). - Being able to articulate all three is a sign of genuine understanding. - The shared language must [[r:live in the code]]: when a business term changes, rename the class as well. A glossary in Confluence while the code still says `status = 2` is a dead language. - When NOT to use it (12-architecture-patterns.domain-driven-design.q3): plain CRUD, a thin domain, a short-lived project, or a team with no DDD experience. Explaining when it is inappropriate matters as much as explaining when it is appropriate. :::

items.q: Bounded contexts: how do you identify the right boundaries?
items.a: A [[b:bounded context]] is the scope within which one model and one vocabulary have consistent meaning. Outside that boundary, the same term may mean something different. **How to find boundaries — in descending order of reliability:** 1. [[g:The language changes meaning]] — the strongest signal. If you must ask *"which Ticket do you mean?"*, you are standing at a boundary. 2. [[g:Different rates of change]] — a part that changes weekly should not be coupled to one that changes once a year. 3. [[g:Ownership]] — under Conway's law, system boundaries tend to align with team boundaries. Going against that means fighting the organization. 4. [[g:Invariants that must be maintained together]] — do [[r:not]] separate things that require immediate consistency (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q2). **A boundary is [[r:not]]:** a database table, a technical module (`web`, `service`), or a JPA entity. Splitting by table is a reliable way to create a distributed monolith (12-architecture-patterns.patterns-principles.q3). :::deep - A bounded context [[o:may]] contain several aggregates; an aggregate [[r:must not]] span two contexts. - In source code, a context should be a [[g:top-level module/package]] (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q8). Spring Modulith can enforce that boundary inside a monolith without extracting a service. - Boundaries are [[o:not fixed]]: redraw them as understanding grows. Redrawing one in a monolith is a refactor; redrawing one after extracting microservices is a project. That is precisely the case for "modular monolith first" (12-architecture-patterns.patterns-principles.q5). - A common mistake is creating a `Common`/`Shared` context for shared entities. It becomes a shared dependency that tightly couples the contexts; a change by either team can break the other; prefer [[g:controlled duplication]] within each context. - For a legacy system that cannot be separated, place an [[o:Anti-Corruption Layer]] (12-architecture-patterns.patterns-principles.q6) at the boundary so the old model does not leak into the new context. - A probing question: *"Are a context and a microservice the same thing?"* — [[r:no]]. A context is a design concept; a service is a deployment unit. A service should contain exactly one context, but a context can live perfectly well inside a monolith. :::

items.q: Context mapping: what relationships can exist between two bounded contexts?
items.a:
After contexts are separated, they still have to communicate. A [[b:context map]] describes the *power relationships* between them — a subject that few people mention but that often appears in senior interviews.
TypeMeaningUse when
Partnershiptwo teams succeed or fail together and collaborate closelythe two contexts must release together
Shared Kernelshare part of the model/coderare — both sides must agree on every change
Customer / Supplierthe upstream serves the downstream, with negotiationboth are in one company and the downstream has influence
Conformistthe downstream accepts the upstream modelthere is no negotiating leverage (a third-party API)
Anti-Corruption Layerthe downstream translates into its own modelthe upstream model is polluted or legacy
Open Host Servicethe upstream exposes a common API to many consumersseveral downstreams use it
Published Languagea shared, versioned contractOpenAPI/Protobuf/event schema
Separate Waysdo not integrate; accept duplicationintegration cost > benefit
In the OTA example, `Booking` ↔ `Payment` is **Customer/Supplier**. `Ticketing` ↔ GDS (Amadeus/Sabre) uses an **ACL**: the GDS model is very old and cannot be changed, so translation belongs at the boundary. A public partner API is **Open Host + Published Language** (17-rest-api-design.contracts-errors-lifecycle.q4). :::deep - [[o:The real value of a context map]] is not its boxes and arrows, but how it exposes *organizational relationships*: "the other team will never change it for us" → Conformist or ACL, not a fantasy Partnership. - [[g:An ACL pays off most]] when integrating with a legacy system or third party: a thin translation layer prevents their polluted model from spreading into your domain. The cost is mapping; the benefits are a clean domain and a single place to change when replacing the provider. - [[r:A Shared Kernel is debt]]: it sounds economical, but forces two teams to coordinate every change. Use it only when one team genuinely owns both contexts. - Integration through [[g:events]] (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q3) is often healthier than synchronous calls: a failing downstream cannot take down the upstream, and the relationship naturally becomes Open Host + Published Language. - Separate Ways is underrated: letting two contexts calculate tax independently can be far cheaper than building a shared `TaxService` that makes everyone wait. - Draw the context map [[o:before]] extracting microservices. Without one, extraction merely splits the system by database table — the recipe for a distributed monolith. :::

items.q: Event storming: how do you run a workshop that reveals the boundaries?
items.a:
Event storming is the most practical way to move from *"nobody knows what the system does"* to a *context map* in a single workshop. Developers, BAs, and domain experts stand together at one wall. **Sticky-note color conventions (standardized; do not invent your own):**
ColorRepresentsExample
OrangeDomain event — something that happened, in the past tenseSeatHeld, PaymentCaptured
BlueCommand — an intention, in the imperative moodHoldSeat, IssueTicket
YellowActor — who initiates itCustomer, customer-service agent
PinkExternal systemGDS, PSP
PurplePolicy — "whenever X, then Y"seat hold expires → release seat
Pale yellowAggregate — where the command landsBooking, Payment
RedHot spot — a disputed or unclear point"how is a partial cancellation charged?"
**Four steps:** 1. Put [[o:all]] domain events on the wall without ordering them yet — whenever someone names one, add it. 2. Arrange them on a [[o:timeline]] from left → right. Contradictions surface immediately; mark them with red notes. 3. Add the command, actor, and external system before each event; add policies between events. 4. Cluster events that tend to occur together → [[g:each cluster is an aggregate]]; where the language changes meaning → [[g:a context boundary]]. :::deep - [[o:Red]] notes are the most valuable output of the workshop. They pinpoint where the business has not reached agreement — exactly where bugs appear when developers guess. - The golden rule: [[r:do not discuss technical solutions]] during the workshop. Someone saying "we'll put this on Kafka" pulls the entire room off course. - Events must be in the [[g:past tense]] (`SeatHeld`, not `HoldSeat`). That sounds minor, but it forces everyone to discuss *what happened* rather than *how to implement it*. - There are three scopes: [[o:big picture]] (the whole company, to find contexts), [[o:process modeling]] (one process), and [[o:design level]] (deriving aggregates and commands directly). Choose the scope that fits the question you need to answer. - Before everyone leaves, turn the result into a [[g:context map]] (24-domain-driven-design.strategic-splitting-the-domain.q3) plus an aggregate list (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q2). Otherwise, the next day all that remains is a photograph nobody reads. - Remote sessions work in Miro or FigJam, but a physical wall is still better because people can stand up, point, and argue more naturally. :::

items.q: Entity vs. Value Object: what distinguishes them, and why are Value Objects more useful than they seem?
items.a:
EntityValue Object
Identityhas an id; distinguished by identityhas no id; equal when all fields are equal
Mutable?yes; its state changes over timeimmutable — replace it to make a change
ExampleBooking, PassengerMoney, SeatNumber, DateRange
Equalityequals by idequals by value
**Value Objects are among the most underused and highest-leverage building blocks.** They turn runtime mistakes into compile-time errors: 
// Before: everything is a primitive — "primitive obsession"
void refund(String bookingId, long amount, String currency) { ... }
refund(seatNo, price, code);          // compiles successfully; completely wrong
//
// After: types express intent
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {
    public Money {
        if (amount.scale() > currency.getDefaultFractionDigits())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid decimal scale for " + currency);
    }
    public Money plus(Money o) {
        if (!currency.equals(o.currency)) throw new DomainException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(amount.add(o.amount), currency);
    }
}
void refund(BookingId id, Money amount) { ... }   // an invalid call does not compile
Adding amounts in two different currencies is now [[g:impossible]], rather than something developers must remember not to do. :::deep - Java 16+ `record` types are an almost perfect fit for VOs: they are immutable, implement `equals`/`hashCode` with value semantics, and provide a compact constructor for validation. Before records, all of that required hand-written code — one reason VOs are less common in older Java codebases. - VOs are the [[g:most natural place]] for small rules: `Money.plus` rejects different currencies, while `DateRange` rejects an end date before its start date. Put a rule here and callers cannot forget to apply it. - Immutability gives [[o:thread safety]] for free (23-java-concurrency-coding.classic-synchronisation-problems.q4): a VO can be shared between threads without locking. - Persist VOs in JPA with `@Embeddable`/`@Embedded`, or an `AttributeConverter` for a single-field VO. If the domain model is separate from persistence entities (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q2), this presents no difficulty at all. - [[r:Do not]] turn every String into a VO. Use one when it carries *rules* or when parameter confusion creates real risk (money, identifiers, seat numbers). A `Name` that merely wraps a `String` without enforcing anything is noise. - Money is [[g:always]] a VO and [[r:never]] a `double` (09-distributed-tx-fintech.correctness-where-money-is-involved.q4) — the canonical example, and one that is universally accepted. :::

items.q: Aggregates: where should the boundary lie, and how large should an aggregate be?
items.a:
An [[b:aggregate]] is a cluster of objects that are loaded, saved, and [[g:kept consistent]] together. The [[b:aggregate root]] is the sole entry point into that cluster. **Vaughn Vernon's four rules — know these and you can answer most aggregate questions:** 1. **Protect invariants within one boundary.** Anything that must be true *immediately* belongs in the same aggregate. 2. **Keep aggregates small.** Start small; enlarge one only when an invariant requires it. 3. **Reference other aggregates by [[o:id]], not by object.** Use `booking.flightId`, not `booking.flight`. 4. **One transaction = one aggregate.** If several aggregates must change, use [[g:eventual consistency]] through domain events (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q3). 
public class Booking {                       // AGGREGATE ROOT
    private final BookingId id;
    private final FlightId flightId;           // rule 3: id only
    private final List<Passenger> passengers;   // inside the boundary
    private BookingStatus status;
    
    public void addPassenger(Passenger p) {      // every change goes through the ROOT
        if (status != DRAFT) throw new DomainException("booking is finalized; passengers cannot be added");
        if (passengers.size() >= 9) throw new DomainException("maximum 9 passengers");
        passengers.add(p);                     // the invariant is enforced HERE
    }
    public List<Passenger> passengers() {
        return List.copyOf(passengers);        // prevents callers from mutating state by bypassing the root
    }
}
:::warn The sizing trap A [[r:large]] aggregate locks the whole cluster: two users modifying different parts still collide, and loading one booking may fetch 500 rows. ::: An aggregate that is [[r:too small]] leaves invariants spanning several aggregates, so events and compensation must maintain them. The deciding question is always: *which invariant absolutely must hold immediately?* :::deep - "A seat must not be booked twice" should [[o:not]] live in a `Flight` aggregate containing 300 seats. That would be a hot aggregate in which everyone booking the same flight contends. - A [[g:database constraint / atomic update]] (16-project-concurrency-whiteboard.presenting-dissecting-the-ota-project.q2) is a better fit. Recognizing this demonstrates where the theory's boundary lies. - References by id have secondary benefits: aggregates serialize compactly, do not pull in half the database, and later service extraction requires almost no domain-model changes. - For concurrency, an aggregate is the natural unit of [[g:optimistic locking]]: keep one `version` column on the root; when two users edit concurrently, the later writer retries (05-db-core-index-lock.transactions-mvcc-locking.q3). - Provide [[g:one repository per aggregate root]], not one per table. A `PassengerRepository` is a sign that `Passenger` has been pulled outside its boundary. - Aggregate boundaries [[o:do not]] correspond one-to-one with tables — one aggregate can span several tables, and the persistence adapter reassembles it (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q2). - Start with [[g:small]] aggregates and merge them when you see an invariant being violated. The reverse direction — splitting a large aggregate — is much harder. :::

items.q: How do domain events differ from integration events, and where should each be published?
items.a:
The distinction is [[g:semantic and contractual]], not “in-process versus Kafka” or “inside versus outside a transaction.”
Domain eventIntegration event
Meaninga business fact meaningful inside a bounded contexta fact/notification intentionally exposed to another context
Contract ownerthe domain model/team; may evolve with the modelproducer and consumers; compatibility and lifecycle are explicit
Deliveryin-memory, persisted, or bothbroker, webhook, stream, file, or another inter-context channel
Payloadstable values needed by local handlers; avoid mutable aggregate referencesconsumer-oriented schema: notification-by-ID or event-carried state are deliberate trade-offs
Reliabilitydepends on the local dispatch/storage designoutbox/relay, retries, idempotency, ordering, schema and observability contract
An aggregate may record immutable domain events without knowing infrastructure. The application layer can handle local reactions and translate selected committed facts into versioned integration events. Not every domain event should leave the bounded context, and an external contract should not leak an internal aggregate object. 
@Transactional
public HoldResult hold(HoldSeatCommand cmd) {
    Booking booking = bookings.get(cmd.bookingId());
    booking.hold(cmd.seat());                  // records SeatHeld domain fact
    bookings.save(booking);
    
    for (DomainEvent event : booking.pullEvents()) {
        localHandlers.handle(event);             // local policy; semantics must be explicit
        integrationMapper.map(event)
            .ifPresent(outbox::append);       // same DB transaction as aggregate
    }
    return HoldResult.ok();
}
// a separate relay publishes committed outbox rows and retries safely
:::deep Transaction timing is an implementation choice. A local domain-event handler may run before commit because it contributes to the same invariant, after commit for a best-effort side effect, or asynchronously from durable storage. Document the failure/rollback semantics. `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)` avoids publishing before rollback but is not durable across a process crash. For reliable external publication, write the integration event/outbox row atomically with the state change, then publish after commit through a relay (09-distributed-tx-fintech.distributed-transaction-patterns.q3). Consumers still need idempotency because commit/publish acknowledgement races create duplicates (08-message-queue.reliability-delivery-semantics.q6). Payload strategy is not “always IDs only.” Notification events minimize coupling and exposure but make consumers call back and depend on current producer state. Event-carried state transfer improves consumer autonomy and historical meaning but duplicates data, increases privacy/schema obligations, and can grow messages. Include the minimum stable facts required by the declared consumer contract, classify sensitive fields, and version compatibility deliberately. Name facts in past tense (`SeatHeld`), include event ID, occurrence time, producer/schema version and domain identifiers where needed, and distinguish occurrence time from publish time. Domain events also do not imply event sourcing; that is a separate persistence decision (12-architecture-patterns.domain-driven-design.q4). :::

items.q: Repository, Factory, and Domain Service: where does each belong, and when is it needed?
items.a:
These three building blocks are often put in the wrong place. **Repository — a collection of aggregates, not a DAO.** 
// RIGHT: interface in domain/application, expressed in domain language
public interface BookingRepository {
    Optional<Booking> findById(BookingId id);
    List<Booking> findExpiredHolds(Instant now);
    void save(Booking booking);            // saves the ENTIRE aggregate
}
// WRONG: a DAO masquerading as a repository
interface BookingRepository {
    void updateStatusById(Long id, int status);   // bypasses the domain
    List<Object[]> findRawJoin();                  // leaks persistence concerns
}
Provide one repository for [[g:each aggregate root]] (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q2), returning [[g:domain objects]] rather than JPA entities (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q2). **Factory — when object creation is complex or must protect invariants at construction time.** If a constructor is sufficient, [[r:do not]] create a factory. Use one when construction draws from several sources, rules select a subtype, or a named operation better expresses intent (`Booking.draftFor(flightId, passengers)`). **Domain Service — only when behavior [[o:does not belong to]] any entity or VO.** Good signals are logic that needs *several* aggregates, or a pure stateless calculation. 
// Appropriate: pricing needs a fare table + fare class + promotions — it belongs to none alone
public class FareCalculator {
    public Money fareFor(Flight f, FareClass c, List<Promotion> promos) { ... }
}
:::warn Domain Service is the most abused If behavior [[o:uses only one aggregate's data]], it belongs on that aggregate. Pushing everything into `XxxDomainService` recreates an anemic domain (12-architecture-patterns.patterns-principles.q3) under a different name. ::: :::deep **Distinguish the three kinds of service:** - An [[b:Application service]] represents a use case, coordinates work, and opens the transaction: (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q3) - A [[b:Domain service]] contains pure business rules and knows nothing about transactions. - An [[b:Infrastructure service]] is an adapter that calls an external system. - They belong to different layers; do not merge them. - Repository methods should be [[g:driven by real use-case needs]]. `findAll()` over a table with tens of millions of rows is a trap; when paginating, use keyset pagination (18-query-optimization.rewriting-the-query-reshaping-the-model.q2). - Complex reporting queries should [[r:not]] be forced into an aggregate repository. They belong to a separate read model (12.8 CQRS), which may query a projection directly. - The Specification pattern wraps a business predicate in a reusable object (`new ExpiredHold(now)`), preventing a repository from accumulating dozens of `findByXxxAndYyy` methods. - Factory and Repository complement each other: a factory creates a [[o:new]] aggregate; a repository reconstructs an [[o:existing]] one. Both return aggregates in valid states. - At interview depth, saying *"a repository is a domain concept; a JPA repository is an implementation detail"* is enough to distinguish the model from habitual Spring Data usage. :::
